title: Traffic Rules, Accidents and Challans
summary: Documents to carry, road rules, what to do after an accident, and how to verify and pay a genuine challan.

body.text: On the road, both drivers and traffic police have clear duties. Knowing them prevents arguments and avoids paying a fine you did not owe.

items: A valid driving licence for the class of vehicle you drive.
Registration certificate (RC), insurance and pollution under control (PUC) certificate.
For commercial vehicles, a permit and a fitness certificate.

body.text: Digital copies in DigiLocker or the mParivahan app are legally accepted as valid documents at a traffic check.

items: Obey signals and road signs: stop at red, go on green, and never block a junction.
Respect the speed limit for the road, and slow down near schools, hospitals and pedestrian crossings.
Never drive on the wrong side or overtake from the left.
Do not use a mobile phone while driving. Use a hands-free device only where it is safe and legal.
Wear a helmet on a two-wheeler, and wear a seat belt in a car, including in the rear.
Stop, switch on hazard lights and help anyone who is injured. Call 108 or 112.
Inform the police if there is injury, death or serious damage. Leaving the scene is a serious offence.
Exchange names, phone numbers, vehicle numbers and insurer details with the other driver.
Note the time, place and, if possible, take photos and note CCTV nearby.
Inform your insurance company within the time stated in your policy, and get a copy of the accident report.
Check the challan on the official e-Challan portal using the challan number or your vehicle number.
Never pay through a link in an SMS. Genuine payments happen only on the official portal or at the police station.
You can pay online, or contest the challan before the designated court if you believe it is wrong.
Always keep the receipt until the matter is closed.

body.text: Never hand over your original documents and walk away. Show them, but do not surrender originals unless there is a legal reason and you get a receipt.
A police officer cannot seize your vehicle or keys for a routine document check. Seizure is allowed only for specific offences, with a receipt.

practicalSteps: Keep digital copies of RC, licence, insurance and PUC in DigiLocker.
Note the challan number, date, place and the officer's details.
Verify and pay online at the official e-Challan portal, or contest it in court within the time allowed.
After any accident, save 108/112, inform your insurer, and keep photos and the accident report.
exceptions: Some documents may be produced later at the police station or online within a set time in certain states.
Helmet and seat-belt rules have limited exemptions, such as for certain medical conditions with proof.

faqs.q: Can the police take away my vehicle keys?
faqs.a: There is no general power to seize keys or your vehicle for a routine document check. Seizure is allowed only for specific offences listed in the law, and you should get a receipt.

faqs.q: Is a photocopy of my documents enough?
faqs.a: Digital copies through DigiLocker or mParivahan are accepted. Otherwise carry originals or certified copies.

sources.label: Parivahan Sewa (Ministry of Road Transport and Highways)

misconceptions.myth: Traffic police can always confiscate my licence on the spot.
misconceptions.fact: For many document offences the law lets you produce the documents later; outright confiscation is limited to specific situations.
